demand.reason: Global tin consumption is estimated at approximately 380,000 metric tons annually, placing it securely within the high-demand band of 100,000–1,000,000 tons.

growth.reason: Tin demand is projected to experience moderate growth (6–12% CAGR) driven by structural expansions in electronics solder for AI chips, rapid capacity scaling in solar PV cell interconnections, and emerging lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery anode technologies.

supplier_concentration.reason:
Mining: Mine production is highly distributed. China is the largest primary producer with 71,000 of the 290,000 tons mined in 2025 (24%), followed by Indonesia (21%), placing the primary extraction diversity firmly in the <30% band (Score 1).


Refining: Processing concentration increases downstream. China imports raw concentrates and accounts for approximately 50% of global smelting and refining output, placing refining diversity within the 50–65% band (Score 3).

reserves.reason:
Time-frame: World reserves are about 6.0 million tons, roughly 21 years of supply at 2025 mine output of 290,000 tons, placing it in the 15–30 year band (Score 4).


Diversification: Indonesia holds 23% of world reserves, China 20%, and Brazil and Burma 12% each. The HHI is about 0.14, below 0.15 (Score 1).

end_use.reason:
Advanced Semiconductors & Computing (+1.0): tin serves as the universal joining material connecting every semiconductor package and printed circuit board globally. Construction & Heavy Industry (+0.5): tinplate steels are foundational for commercial food and industrial packaging. Electrification & Transport (+1.0): massive solder dependencies exist across EV battery management systems and power electronics. Defense & National Security (+1.5): essential for military electronics assemblies and treated as a formal strategic material by the US DoD. Healthcare & Biomedical (+1.0): advanced PCB assemblies govern sophisticated life-saving medical devices.


Sector presence scores total 5.0 across 5 qualifying sectors. The breadth bonus for 5 sectors adds +2.0, yielding an objective composite score of 7.0.

substitutability_recyclability.reason:
Substitutability: Bismuth-based and silver-based solders, alongside conductive epoxy adhesives, are commercially deployed alternatives but carry moderate performance trade-offs in thermal cycling and cost, representing viable substitutions that industries can adapt to within 1-2 years (Score 2).


Recyclability: Global secondary production captures approximately 18,000 tons (about 22-27% of apparent consumption) primarily via industrial detinning plants recovering bulk tinplate scrap. End-of-life electronics recovery remains economically marginal. This establishes a functional secondary supply chain, placing it in the 20–40% moderate recycling tier.

extraction_refining.reason: Tin extraction and refining rely on simple and widely accessible technologies. Placer deposits utilize standard dredging or gravity concentration, while smelting occurs in reverberatory or electric arc furnaces at low temperatures without generating toxic byproducts or necessitating exotic proprietary chemistry.

upcoming_projects.reason: The project pipeline is thin but active. Reopening legacy sites like South Crofty (UK) and expansions at existing mines (DRC, Peru) exist, but they remain small relative to overarching demand and face execution risks, capable of adding 5–10% to supply with realistic first production 5–7 years away.

india_position.reason:
Import Dependence: India possesses no large-scale domestic mine production, extracting only token quantities from small placer deposits in Jharkhand. While domestic secondary recycling is scaling, internal production satisfies only 10–20% of industrial consumption, making the nation >80% import-dependent and pacing at the marginal domestic production band.


Strategic Posture: Tin is officially recognized on India's critical minerals list and targeted for PLI electronics expansions. However, no specific KABIL supply mandates or binding foreign equity investments exist, aligning with declared strategic intent at an early stage.

price_volatility.reason: Tin prices are subject to highly opaque and volatile shifts. Between 2020 and 2024, LME pricing swung from ~$15,000/t to a record $48,000/t before crashing and subsequently spiking again by 46% following militia-led mining halts in Myanmar. These sudden >100% price movements and severe supply shocks demonstrate high volatility.

capability.name: Tin
capability.next_move: Work the Chhattisgarh deposits at scale and recover tin from solder and tinplate scrap.
capability.what_india_has: Small mine output in Dantewada, Chhattisgarh (45 t of concentrate in 2022-23) and one smelter at Jagdalpur (17 t of metal); 103,757 t of contained tin in resources, 64% of the ore in Haryana; a tin block auctioned in Chhattisgarh.

stages.world: China 71,000 t and Indonesia 61,000 t of 290,000 t (2025); Peru, Brazil and DR Congo next.
stages.india: 45,429 kg of concentrate in 2022-23, all from Chhattisgarh; the state corporation buys ore collected by local tribal people.
Precious Minerals and Smelting, a joint venture with the state mineral corporation, at Jagdalpur: 17,160 kg of tin metal in 2022-23.
Tinplate (The Tin Plate Company of India, Jamshedpur) and solder, made from imported metal.

stages.world: Electronics solder, food cans, PVC stabilisers.
stages.india: Solder is now the largest use, then tinplate; 13,792 t of tin and alloys were imported in 2022-23.
